title: Numbers 17:1–13
context: After Korah’s rebellion and the plague that followed the people’s complaint against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16), the LORD settles the question of who may serve as priest. Each tribal leader’s rod is placed before the covenant in the Tent of Meeting, and overnight Aaron’s rod for the house of Levi sprouts, blossoms and bears ripe almonds. The rod is kept before the covenant as a lasting sign against rebellion, and the people respond with fear that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die. Versification: English 16:36–50 is Hebrew 17:1–15, and English 17:1–13 is Hebrew 17:16–28; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read this as shared ground: God chooses and confirms those he appoints to priestly service, ends grumbling by a clear sign, and provides mercy so that his people need not die; the choice here concerns an office, not individual salvation.

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the resolution to the crisis of Numbers 16 begins with the LORD speaking. The dispute over the priesthood will be settled by God’s own word, not by human argument.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD taking the initiative to answer the rebellion. Readers in both traditions commonly see this as a gracious response to grumbling that had already brought judgment.

verses.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and take rods from them, one for each fathers’ house, of all their princes according to their fathers’ houses, twelve rods. Write each man’s name on his rod.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the twelve rods, each marked with a tribal leader’s name, as a fair and public test. Every tribe is represented, so the outcome cannot be dismissed as favoritism.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the careful procedure God’s concern to make his choice unmistakable to all Israel. Both traditions generally read the rods as standing for the tribes and their leaders.

verses.text: You shall write Aaron’s name on Levi’s rod. There shall be one rod for each head of their fathers’ houses.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Aaron’s name is written on Levi’s rod, placing his claim alongside the other tribes. The question raised by Korah is put openly before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of Aaron’s name as preparing for God’s confirmation of the priesthood he has already appointed. Readers in both traditions commonly see the test as vindicating rather than creating Aaron’s office.

verses.text: You shall lay them up in the Tent of Meeting before the covenant, where I meet with you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the rods laid before the covenant, where God meets with Moses, as placing the decision in God’s presence. The sign will come from the place of God’s word and nearness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the setting before the covenant as underlining that the outcome rests with God. Both traditions generally treat the Tent as the place where God makes his will known.

verses.text: It shall happen that the rod of the man whom I shall choose shall bud. I will make the murmurings of the children of Israel, which they murmur against you, cease from me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see “the man whom I shall choose” as God appointing someone to a specific office, not a statement about personal salvation. God also aims to end the murmuring that endangered the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read this choice as vocational, God’s calling to the priesthood (compare Hebrews 5:4). Readers in both traditions commonly agree that the verse is about office, and they see God’s purpose as merciful: to stop the complaints before more judgment fell.

verses.text: Moses spoke to the children of Israel; and all their princes gave him rods, for each prince one, according to their fathers’ houses, a total of twelve rods. Aaron’s rod was among their rods.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the leaders cooperate fully, each giving a rod. The test is carried out openly and with the people’s participation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the leaders submitting their claims to God’s judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing a fair process in which Aaron’s rod is treated like the others.

verses.text: Moses laid up the rods before the LORD in the Tent of the Testimony.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Moses carefully obeying the LORD’s instructions. The rods are left before God, and the people must wait for his answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the outcome now lies entirely with God. Readers in both traditions generally see the waiting as part of trusting God’s decision.

verses.text: On the next day, Moses went into the Tent of the Testimony; and behold, Aaron’s rod for the house of Levi had sprouted, budded, produced blossoms, and bore ripe almonds.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers marvel at the abundance of the sign: the rod sprouts, buds, blossoms and bears ripe almonds overnight. God answers with a sign of life, not of death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a dead stick brought to life as God’s unmistakable confirmation of Aaron. Some readers in both traditions see in it a picture of resurrection life, while generally holding that connection as an interpretive reflection rather than the text’s stated point.

verses.text: Moses brought out all the rods from before the LORD to all the children of Israel. They looked, and each man took his rod.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see each leader taking back his own rod, a quiet admission that God has decided. The evidence is plain for all to see.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the public display as settling the matter before the whole people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s choice was clear, not hidden.

verses.text: The LORD said to Moses, “Put back the rod of Aaron before the covenant, to be kept for a token against the children of rebellion; that you may make an end of their complaining against me, that they not die.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Aaron’s rod kept before the covenant as a lasting reminder meant to prevent further rebellion and death. God’s purpose in the sign is protective as well as corrective.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the preserved rod as a memorial of God’s appointment and a warning to the rebellious (compare Hebrews 9:4). Readers in both traditions generally agree that God aims to end complaining “that they not die.”

verses.text: Moses did so. As the LORD commanded him, so he did.
verses.arminianNotes:
Arminian readers note Moses’ simple, complete obedience: “As the LORD commanded him, so he did.” He places the rods without adding a rite of his own. The sign that follows will rest on this faithfulness, not on any extra ceremony Moses invents.

Faithful leaders do what God commands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Moses as a model of obedience to God’s word. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a brief but important note of faithfulness.

verses.text: The children of Israel spoke to Moses, saying, “Behold, we perish! We are undone! We are all undone!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people’s cry, “we perish,” as a sudden awareness of the danger of approaching a holy God. Their earlier complaining has turned to fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a sinful people coming to sense their unworthiness before God’s holiness. Readers in both traditions commonly see this fear as a true but incomplete response that God answers in the next chapter.

verses.text: Everyone who keeps approaching the LORD’s tabernacle, dies! Will we all perish?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people’s question as an honest cry for a way to live near God without dying. Numbers 18 answers it by appointing priests and Levites to guard the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as pointing to the need for a mediator. Many in both traditions connect this need with Christ, through whom believers draw near with confidence (Hebrews 10:19–22), while generally recognizing that the text first speaks of Israel’s situation.
